_readme: P1 Grand Challenges (decided 2026-10-02; master handoff §14, capability ladder §4.1 and §26): small problems prove principles, big projects change capability. A challenge opens when the work has raised its question: 'routes' lists the ways it can come up (each route's 'requires' must all hold; any route will do; the first that holds, in order, opens it, once), so no Grand Challenge hangs on a single client (hardening pass 2026-10-04). The single-route form 'opens'/'openCategory'/'openText' still loads; each stage is a chunky project (months, Attention a month, gold in aurei at AD 155 prices) that moves a capability, never a run of micro-scenes. A stage may need a resource Rome doesn't hand a stranger: the 'source' requirements (people.json syntax) get it at the stated price, otherwise it costs 'withoutSource' times as much. Stages may name 'also' (further capabilities moved, in order) and 'needsPerson' as 'a|b' (the first if here, else the second, with 'slowerWithout' extra months and 'standInText' in place of the stage's text). 'consequence' names a triggered event (events.json) offered when the challenge is done. Amounts PROPOSED P1-10 and P1-15.

challenges.name: Measurement and standards
challenges.question: Can another workshop make a part that fits without seeing the original?

routes.text: Cassianus's pump has a seat that wore out. The bronzesmith on the Clivus cut a new one by eye, and it leaks. Your seats were cut to your own foot and your own rule; his are cut to his. Until two shops measure the same way, every repair is a new pump.

A tooth breaks off the ratchet on Aemilius's drum. The smith at the Emporium cuts a new pawl from your drawing, and it rides up over the ratchet instead of catching. Your drawing says a finger and a half; his finger is not yours, and nor is his foot. Until two shops measure the same way, every repair is a new hoist.

Two calices on your bench, both stamped as one quinaria: the water office's, and the one Gaius cast to your rule. Timed on the same bucket, Gaius's passes a sixth more. Neither man cheated. Each measured by his own finger, and Rome has as many fingers as plumbers. Until two shops measure the same way, every allotment is an argument.

Philippus's stopcock sticks, and the plumber who knows the fuller turns him a new plug. It won't seat in your bronze body. Both of you cut to a finger's width; his plumber's rule is a hair longer than yours, and the water finds the hair. Until two shops measure the same way, every repair is a new stopcock.

stages.name: A master foot in hard bronze

resource.name: tin bronze for a master that won't wear
resource.note: Good tin comes through Ostia, and the guild's shippers sell it to men they've eaten with. A stranger pays twice.

stages.text: The founder pours the bar twice before it comes out without a flaw. You file the ends square and mark the foot and its sixteen fingers. It is heavier than anything it will ever measure.

stages.name: Two shops agree on the foot
stages.needsText: Another shop has to agree to work to your foot, and no shop will take a stranger's word for it. You need someone who knows the shops: a guild man who has seen your work, or a smith who has.
stages.text: Felix brings the bronzesmith from the Clivus and a fitter from Ostia to your bench. They check their rules against your bar, argue for an afternoon, and go home with copies. A month later the parts they cut match yours.
stages.standInText: Gaius brings a fitter from Ostia he has sold bronze to for years, and the least dishonest plumber from the water office. They check their rules against your bar, argue for an afternoon, and go home with copies. A month later the parts they cut match yours.

stages.name: Fit and no-fit gauges in hard steel

resource.name: Noric steel that holds an edge
resource.note: The best steel comes over the Alps from Noricum, and the merchants who carry it sell to guild members first.

stages.text: Two plugs for every bore: one that must go in, one that must not. The smith hardens them in oil and swears at the one that cracks. The second pair holds.

stages.name: A part made in another shop fits
stages.text: The fitter at Ostia cuts a part to the gauges and sends it up the river in a box. It drops into its place at your bench without a file touching it. The bronzesmith asks for a set of gauges of his own and pays for them.

challenges.completeText: Three shops now cut parts to one set of gauges, and a part from one fits a machine from another. Nobody calls it a standard. They say the parts are cut to the foreigner's foot.

challenges.name: Powered workshops
challenges.question: Can one power source reliably drive several useful workshop machines, with components and maintenance Roman craftsmen can reproduce?
challenges.openText: Rome already grinds its grain by water; the mills on the Janiculum turn all day. What no one has done is put several different machines on one wheel and keep them running with parts any millwright can cut and change.

stages.name: A wheel and a race to build on
stages.needsText: You need a millwright who knows the hill and will talk to you.
stages.text: Aulus walks you down the race. Here the water comes smooth; there it spills over the boards and the wheel stutters. The mill with the clever extra gears is the one that fouls with mud every spring. He picks a wheel below the third mill: an old one, easy water, an owner who owes him money.

stages.name: A shaft on replaceable bearing blocks

resource.name: bronze for the bearing shells
resource.note: Good bearing bronze comes through the Ostia merchants, who sell to guild members first.

stages.text: A long oak shaft on bronze shells that sit in split blocks, so a worn shell can be knocked out and another dropped in. Aulus has Gaius cut the shells to your gauge, six alike. "Grease this before the wheel starts. Every morning," Aulus says. "Or buy another bearing."

stages.name: One real machine on the shaft
stages.needsText: You need a shop that will put its own work on the wheel.
stages.text: Gaius's lathe goes on the shaft first, belted from a pulley, and turns bearing shells for the next block. He stands back from it with his arms folded. When the first shell comes off true he picks it up, turns it over, and puts it down without a word.

stages.name: Heavy work and hot bearings
stages.text: Under a real load the far bearing runs hot enough to smoke. Aulus cuts a groove so the grease feeds itself and has Gaius make the shells wider. A rope drive with a lever to slacken it lets one machine stop while the shaft turns on. "Move that bench," Aulus says. "Someone will reach across the shaft for a hammer." Then: "Tie your sleeves."

stages.name: A second, different task: boring and grinding

resource.name: Noric steel for the cutters
resource.note: Cutters that hold an edge need Noric steel, and the merchants who carry it sell to guild members first.

stages.text: A boring bar on the second pulley, held rigid between two blocks, and a grinding wheel on the third. The bar bores a cylinder straighter than any hand. The wheel takes the rough off castings that Gaius's men used to file for a day. His men watch it the way men watch a horse they haven't decided about.

stages.name: Three months under a real load
stages.slowerText: Without Marcus to keep the tally of every stop, Gaius keeps it, badly, and slowly.
stages.text: Three months of real orders on the wheel. The tally book fills: a shell changed in the second week, a rope that stretched, a day lost to a flood in the race and a day to a festival. By the end Aulus's sons at Ostia ask for the drawings, and a millwright Aulus never trained builds a shaft from them that runs.

challenges.completeText: One wheel drives a lathe, a boring bar and a grinder, and the parts that wear can be cut and changed by men who never met you. Nobody calls it anything. The millwrights call it Aulus's shaft.
